title: Your first HTTP server
idea: `http.createServer` lets you answer web requests with one handler function. Node calls it once per request, with `req` to read and `res` to reply.

analogy.text: A receptionist with one instruction card. Each visitor hands over a note, gets a written reply, and the receptionist waits for the next.
analogy.breaks: Replies can overlap: a second visitor may arrive before the first is answered.

points: `server.listen(port)` opens a numbered door on your machine; `0` picks a free one.
`req` carries the `method`, `url` and `headers` of the request.
`res.writeHead(status, headers)` sets status and headers; `res.end(body)` sends the body and finishes.
A listening server keeps the process alive until you call `server.close()`.

steps.caption: The server is already listening. A client sends `GET /hi` to its port.
Node's `http` code reads the request and builds `req` and `res` for it.
Node calls your handler once with `req` and `res`. This one logs the request.
The handler calls `res.writeHead` and `res.end('hello')`. That completes the response.
`http` writes the status line, headers and body to the connection.
The client reads the response and prints it. The server keeps listening for the next request.
Now suppose a handler forgets `res.end()`. The request reaches it as before.
Nothing is sent back. The client keeps waiting for a reply.

code.title: A server that calls itself
code.caption: A server on a free port, called twice with `fetch`, which a later lesson covers. Step through it, then press Run.

walk.text: `createServer` takes your handler. Node calls it for every request.
`req.method` and `req.url` tell you what the client asked for.
`writeHead` sets the status and headers. Call it before the body.
`res.end` sends the body and finishes the response.
`listen(0)` opens any free port. The callback runs when the server is ready.
The script calls its own server twice with `fetch` and prints each answer.
`close` stops the server so the script can exit.

pitfalls: Call `res.end()` on every path; a handler that forgets it leaves the client hanging.
Set status and headers before `res.end()`; later `writeHead` or `setHeader` calls throw `ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT`.
Listen on `0` in tests; a fixed port that is taken fails with `EADDRINUSE`.

quiz.why: `writeHead(201)` sets the status. `res.end(req.method)` sends the method name as the body, and the client sent POST.

takeaway: A response is finished only when your handler calls `res.end()`.

starters: What does `server.listen` do, and why does it need a port?
Why does my server say EADDRINUSE?
Do I need Express, or is `node:http` enough?
